As the most massive of the eight planets, the gravitational influence of Jupiter has helped shape the Solar System. With the exception of [Mercury](/wiki/Mercury_(planet) "Mercury (planet)"), the orbits of the system's planets lie closer to Jupiter's [orbital plane](/wiki/Orbital_plane_(astronomy) "Orbital plane (astronomy)") than the Sun's [equatorial plane](/wiki/Celestial_equator "Celestial equator"). The [Kirkwood gaps](/wiki/Kirkwood_gap "Kirkwood gap") in the [asteroid belt](/wiki/Asteroid_belt "Asteroid belt") are mostly caused by Jupiter,[[159]](#cite_note-165) and the planet may have been responsible for the [Late Heavy Bombardment](/wiki/Late_Heavy_Bombardment "Late Heavy Bombardment") in the inner Solar System's history.[[160]](#cite_note-166)

In addition to its moons, Jupiter's gravitational field controls numerous [asteroids](/wiki/Asteroid "Asteroid") that have settled around the [Lagrangian points](/wiki/Lagrangian_point "Lagrangian point") that precede and follow the planet in its orbit around the Sun. These are known as the [Trojan asteroids](/wiki/Trojan_asteroid "Trojan asteroid"), and are divided into [Greek](/wiki/List_of_Trojan_asteroids_(Greek_camp) "List of Trojan asteroids (Greek camp)") and [Trojan](/wiki/List_of_Trojan_asteroids_(Trojan_camp) "List of Trojan asteroids (Trojan camp)") "camps" to honour the *[Iliad](/wiki/Iliad "Iliad")*. The first of these, [588 Achilles](/wiki/588_Achilles "588 Achilles"), was discovered by [Max Wolf](/wiki/Max_Wolf "Max Wolf") in 1906; since then more than two thousand have been discovered.[[161]](#cite_note-167) The largest is [624 Hektor](/wiki/624_Hektor "624 Hektor").[[162]](#cite_note-168)

*Crocus* forms a monophyletic [clade](/wiki/Clade "Clade"), with a basal [polytomy](/wiki/Polytomy "Polytomy") of four subclades. The first clade (A) corresponding to section *Crocus*, but including *C. sieberi* and several closely related species (originally included in section *Nudiscapus* series *Reticulati*). The remaining three clades (B-D) include all the remaining species of section *Nudiscapus*. Of these, B and C are small, corresponding to series *Orientales* and *Carpetani* respectively, with all remaining series in the large D clade. The exception is *C. caspius*, originally in series *Biflori*, which [segregates](/wiki/Segregate_(taxonomy) "Segregate (taxonomy)") in clade B. Thus, although division of the genus into two sections is well supported, no single morphological character defines these two groups. The *C. sieberi* group are assumed to have lost their prophyll secondarily. Of the series, eight could be shown to be monophyletic; *Crocus*, *Kotschyani* and *Scardici* (section *Crocus*) and *Aleppici*, *Carpetani*, *Laevigati*, *Orientalis* and *Speciosi* (section *Nudiscapus*). Flowering season did not correspond to molecular groupings and nor did any of the previously used morphological characteristics, indicating a high degree of [homoplasy](/wiki/Homoplasy "Homoplasy"), in which traits are gained or lost independently in different lineages. The remainder of the series could not be supported as natural groupings. Mathew's concept of subspecies status within *C. biflorus* could not be supported, each being considered a separate species, resulting in the genus having at least 150 species.[[15]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarpke_et_al2013-15)
